key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Family & Protective Services
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of Texas, Third District (Austin)
key_cases.holding: A person named in a central-registry abuse finding need not exhaust the Department's administrative review (ARIF, then Office of Consumer Affairs or SOAH) before suing in district court, because Family Code § 261.309 makes that remedy non-exclusive.
key_cases.relevance: The leading published Texas decision on the process due to a person placed on the central registry by a 'reason to believe' finding.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the legislature has not vested exclusive jurisdiction over such complaints in the Department

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Fabricating evidence of child sexual abuse that causes a child's removal violates the parents' substantive due process right to family integrity and shocks the conscience.
key_cases.relevance: A substantiated finding built on fabricated evidence supports a substantive due process claim, not merely an administrative appeal.
key_cases.quote: the district court was correct in holding that a teacher's fabrication of sexual abuse against a student's father shocks the contemporary conscience

key_cases.holding: A mental-health professional who examines a child for abuse owes no professional duty of care to a third party — here the accused father — to avoid negligently misdiagnosing the child, and the affidavit she filed in the family court was privileged as a judicial-proceeding communication.
key_cases.relevance: A substantiated finding built on a clinician's diagnosis cannot be attacked through a negligence suit against the clinician; the parent's remedy lies inside the agency and court process, not in tort.
key_cases.quote: We hold that a mental health professional owes no professional duty of care to a third party to not negligently misdiagnose a condition of a patient.

state_agency.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

notice_requirements.timing: In writing before the department conducts an interview with an alleged perpetrator; the person signs the written notice to acknowledge receipt (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))
content_required: That the person may request an administrative review of the department's findings under Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309 (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))

Administrative review of a disputed determination of whether child abuse or neglect occurred is conducted by a department employee in administration who was not involved in and did not directly supervise the investigation, and the review must sustain, alter, or reverse the department's original findings (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(c))

The review must be conducted as soon as possible but not later than the 45th day after the date the department receives the request, unless the department has good cause for extending the deadline or a related court proceeding or criminal investigation is pending (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(d))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091; the department must document in the case file that it provided the notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(b)). A person is not required to exhaust the review remedy before pursuing a judicial remedy provided by law (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(e)), and when a finding is overturned the department must remove the person's name from the central registry not later than the 10th business day after it receives notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.002(b)(3))
